chunks.text: In short
If you have a Google Business Profile and you are satisfied with it doing all the work, the answer might genuinely be no.
Where G B P falls short: it cannot carry your story, your real menu copy, or any direct-relationship channel.
The five-minute test that tells you whether you need one, and what it would actually cost if you do.
Leer este artículo en español →
The short answer.
Probably yes. But not for the reason most web designers will tell you, and not in the way you are probably imagining.

I’m front-of-house manager at a restaurant in the Dmv. I also build websites for restaurants through my studio, Muntin Digital. That means I have been on both sides of this question, the side that is paying for a site and the side that is selling one. So here is the version I would give a friend who asked me at the bar after a shift: you need a website if your Google Business Profile is not enough to answer the questions a first-time customer has before they walk in. For most restaurants, it is not.
What your Google Business Profile already does.
Before we talk about websites, let us be honest about what Google already gives you for free:

Hours and location. Google Maps shows your hours, your address, and a one-tap directions button. For "where are you and when are you open," Google handles this better than your website does, because it is where people are already looking.
Phone number. Tap to call, right from the listing. No extra click needed.
Photos. Customers upload their own. You can add official ones. Google surfaces them prominently.
Reviews. The most powerful trust signal in local search, and it lives on Google, not on your site.
Reservation links. If you use OpenTable, Resy, or another major platform, Google shows a "Reserve a table" button directly in the listing.

If your restaurant is a taco truck, a pop-up , or a counter-service spot where the entire customer journey is "see you on Google Maps, drive there, order at the counter", a website might genuinely be optional. Google Business Profile handles the essentials, and you could spend that website budget on better signage, a faster P O S, or a neighborhood postcard campaign instead.
Where Google Business Profile falls short.
But here is what Google does not give you, and this is where the website earns its keep:

Your full menu, the way you want it. Google's built-in menu editor is plain text, no photos, no seasonal flags, no wine descriptions, no prix fixe formatting. It works for basic dishes-and-prices, but if your menu is part of the experience (tasting notes, pairings, rotating specials), Google's version undersells you.

Your story. Who cooks the food? Where do you source? Why does this restaurant exist? None of that lives on Google. A first-time visitor decides based on vibes, and Google's vibes are "beige listing with user-uploaded photos."

Online ordering you control. Google can link to third-party ordering (DoorDash, Uber Eats), but every order through a third party costs you 15, 30% in commission fees. Your own site can route orders through your P O S at a fraction of that cost.
Private events, catering, and group inquiries. There is no Google Business Profile field for "we do private buyouts on Mondays." That is a page on your website, or it does not exist at all.

S E O for long-tail discovery. Google Business Profile is already the primary driver of the local map pack, when someone searches "Italian restaurant near me," your G B P listing is what appears. But a website with real content helps you rank in the organic results below the map, and for more specific queries like "restaurants with private dining Bethesda" or "best brunch Silver Spring gluten free." Those long-tail searches are where a website earns traffic that G B P alone cannot capture.

The first visit, walked as five steps, showing where a Google Business Profile alone stops carrying the customer. Step one, get found, covered: G B P handles hours, directions, tap-to-call, photos, and reviews better than your website would, because it is where people already look. Step two, read the menu, underdelivered: G B P’s built-in menu editor is plain text only, no photos, no seasonal flags, no wine descriptions, so a menu that is part of the experience gets undersold. Step three, choose you over the block, leaking: there is no G B P field for who cooks, where you source, or why the restaurant exists, so the tiebreak against the place next door happens on user-uploaded vibes. Step four, order or book the big party, leaking: third-party ordering links cost fifteen to thirty percent commission per order, and private buyouts and catering have no G B P field at all. Step five, come back for the specific thing, leaking: long-tail searches like restaurants with private dining Bethesda or best brunch Silver Spring gluten free route past the map pack and land nowhere without a site. The journey starts covered and ends leaking, and the leak points are exactly the jobs a website exists to do.
The question is not "do I need a website?" It is "is there anything my customers need to know that Google Business Profile cannot tell them?"
You need a website if your Google Business Profile cannot answer the question a first-time customer is about to ask. For most independent restaurants, it cannot.
The five-minute test.
Open your Google Business Profile listing on your phone as if you were a first-time customer. Ask yourself:
Can I read the full menu without downloading a P D F?
Can I make a reservation without leaving Google?
Can I order food for pickup without paying a third-party commission?
Can I find out about private dining or catering ?
Can I understand what makes this restaurant different from the three others on the same block?

If you answered "no" to two or more, you need a website. Not because a designer told you so, because your customers have questions that Google cannot answer, and every unanswered question is a diner who went somewhere else.

The five-minute test as a five-question diagnostic you can score. Open your own Google Business Profile on a phone, as a first-time customer would, and count one point for every no. Question one: can you read the full menu without downloading a P D F? Yes means dishes and prices sit in plain text on the listing; no means a sunlit phone cannot read your menu. Question two: can you make a reservation without leaving Google? Yes means a working Reserve a table button wired to OpenTable, Resy, or another major provider; no means an 11 PM booking impulse dies at call us tomorrow. Question three: can you order pickup without paying a third-party commission? Yes means a direct link routing to your P O S; no means every order hands fifteen to thirty percent to a middleman. Question four: can you find private dining or catering information? Yes means buyouts, group menus, and minimums are written down somewhere; no means the inquiry goes to a competitor who has the page. Question five: can you tell what makes this restaurant different from the three others on the block? Yes means the story and sourcing are visible; no means the beige listing decides. Zero or one no, G B P is doing the job. Two or more, you need a website.
When you genuinely do not need one.
I promised honesty, so here it is. You can skip the website if:
You are a pop-up or seasonal concept that might not exist in six months. Put that budget into signage and a strong Instagram instead.
Your entire model is counter-service with no menu complexity. A taco window, a coffee cart, a single-item concept. Google Maps + a phone number is genuinely all you need.

You just opened and the concept is still changing. Wait until the menu settles and you know what Tuesdays look like before investing in a site. A Wix placeholder is fine for the first six to twelve months while you figure out who you are.
You are in a food hall. The food hall's website handles discovery. You just need to show up in their vendor list.

For everyone else, full-service restaurants, multi-location groups, places with private dining programs, anyone who wants to rank in discovery searches, anyone paying third-party commission on orders they could route directly, a website pays for itself. The question is just when and how much.
What a good restaurant website actually costs.

If you have decided you need one, the next question is always about money. The honest range for an independent restaurant: 2,500 dollars to 15,000 dollars depending on scope, with most single-location places landing between 5,000 dollars and 9,000 dollars. I wrote an entire breakdown of what drives the price, what each line item costs, and three real-world example bundles, read the full pricing post here .

The honest cost range for an independent restaurant website. The lower bound is twenty-five hundred dollars for a template-based one-pager. The typical range for a single-location restaurant is five thousand to nine thousand dollars. The upper bound is fifteen thousand dollars for fully custom builds with deeper scope. Most independents land in the middle band.

The short version: a good site pays for itself within a few months through recovered reservations, eliminated third-party ordering fees, and discovery traffic that did not exist before. The math almost always works, I show it with real numbers in that post.
Key takeaways
G B P gives you discoverability and basic info; a website gives you the relationship.
Without a website, you are renting your audience from Google, fine until Google's algorithm changes.
The five-minute test: if every regular found you a different way, you do not need a site yet.
If you genuinely do not need one, do the 30-minute G B P audit and walk away.
When you do need one, a 2,500 dollars template site is enough to start; full custom comes when the room demands it.
